nt: The author is speaking of a whole, **all of Israel**, to mean a part of that whole, representatives of the various Israelite tribes who **gathered to David**. The tribal representatives are using the term **Behold** to focus David’s attention on what they are about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen]

Here, **we are your bone and your flesh** was a common expression that the tribal representatives were using to affirm to David that they were related by descent from a common ancestor. If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [we are your blood relatives]

The tribal representatives are speaking of a commander’s first and last actions in a military campaign, **bringing out** the soldiers to war and **bringing** them back **in** afterward, in order to mean military campaigns as a whole. וַ⁠יֹּאמֶר֩ יְהוָ֨ה אֱלֹהֶ֜י⁠ךָ לְ⁠ךָ֗ אַתָּ֨ה תִרְעֶ֤ה אֶת־עַמִּ⁠י֙ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְ⁠אַתָּה֙ תִּהְיֶ֣ה נָגִ֔יד עַ֖ל עַמִּ֥⁠י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [And Yahweh your God told you that you would shepherd his people Israel and that you would become the ruler over his people Israel.]
אַתָּ֨ה תִרְעֶ֤ה אֶת־עַמִּ⁠י֙ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְ⁠אַתָּה֙ תִּהְיֶ֣ה נָגִ֔יד עַ֖ל עַמִּ֥⁠י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

When Yahweh spoke to David as the representatives describe, he was stating the pronoun **you** separately in both of these instances, even though the verbs translated as **you will shepherd** and **you will become** already included this meaning, to emphasize that none other than David would do these things. If speakers of your language would use explicit pronouns for this purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [You are the one who will shepherd my people Israel, and you are the one who will become the ruler over my people Israel]
אַתָּ֨ה תִרְעֶ֤ה אֶת־עַמִּ⁠י֙ אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל וְ⁠אַתָּה֙ תִּהְיֶ֣ה נָגִ֔יד עַ֖ל עַמִּ֥⁠י יִשְׂרָאֵֽל

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition, and it would be good to show this to your readers by including both phrases in your translation rather than combining them. It may be clearer in your language to connect the phrases with a word other than **and** in order to show that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. Alternate translation: [You are the one who will shepherd my people Israel; indeed, you are the one who will become the ruler over my people Israel]

Yahweh is speaking as if David would actually **shepherd** the people of Israel, as though they were sheep. This image compares the way a shepherd cares for and guides his sheep to the way a king should care for and lead his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [You are the one who will care for and guide my people Israel]

The author is not referring to a specific **Jebusite**. He means the Jebusites who lived in this fortified area in Jerusalem. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use expressions that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And the Jebusites]

The author assumes that readers will understand that by **the dwellers of the land**, he means that the Jebusites were among the original inhabitants of the land of Canaan, before the Israelites arrived. In [2 Samuel 23:8](../2sa/23/08.md), this man may be called Josheb Basshebeth the Tahchemonite, or the text may mean “the Tahchemonite who sat in the chief seat.” Many scholars believe that 1 Chronicles presents the more ordinary forms of his personal and clan names.

The author is using the adjective **Thirty** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. The phrase **the Thirty** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. There is, however, a correction in the margin of the text that Hebrew scribes have recommended. You may want to follow this correction in your translation, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [the officers]

The author is using the adjective **300** as a noun to mean a certain kind of thing, a person, and specifically an enemy soldier. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [300 enemy soldiers]

The author is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. David is using the question form to express his strong desire for water from the well. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I wish that someone would give me water from the well of Bethlehem that is at the gate!]

The term for **waters** is always plural in Hebrew. Different languages may need to use a singular form in certain contexts, as the ULT does in many other places and as the UST does here. However, since the Hebrew says **them** in the next verse, the ULT uses a plural form here. If your language would use a plural form in such a context, it would be appropriate to do that in your translation.

See the discussion in the introduction to 1 Chronicles of the Hebrew instructional form that the ULT represents with the English helping verb “shall.” Alternate translation: [Should I drink the blood of these men with their lives]

David is using the question form to emphasize that he should not do what he describes. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I should certainly not drink the blood of these men with their lives!]

David is using **with their lives** as a common expression of his culture to mean “who risked their lives.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the blood of these men who risked their lives]

David is speaking as if the water that the men brought were actually their **blood**. He means that the water represents the danger into which these men put their lives to get it for him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [this water that I am pouring out, since the blood of these men could just as easily have been poured out when they risked their lives to get it]
Here the word **For** introduces not a reason but an explanation. Alternate translation: [After all,]

The pronoun **them** refers to the “waters” the men got for David (v. 18). It may be more natural in some languages to use a singular pronoun. Alternate translation: [they brought it with their lives] or [they risked their lives to get it for me]

The author is offering a summary of the stories he has just related. This signals the end of this section about these **three warriors**. Use a natural way in your language to offer a summary that concludes a section. Alternate translation: [Those are some of the things that David’s three mighty warriors did for him] or [So ends the account of what these three warriors did]

nt: The author seems to be describing two different groups of three warriors. In order to distinguish between them, the ULT treats the word **Three** as a title (uppercase) when it describes the great warriors of the first rank, Jashobeam ([11:11](../11/11.md)), Eleazar ([11:12](../11/12.md)), and an unnamed third warrior. It treats the word **three** as a description (lowercase) when it describes the great warriors of the second rank, Abishai (here and in the next verse), Benaiah ([11:22–25](../11/22.md)), and another unnamed warrior. Your language may have a convention of its own that you could use to distinguish between these groups, or you could use descriptive phrases, as the UST does.

The author is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he was** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the identify of **Abishai** as the man who was the **head** of these warriors. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [he was the one who was the head of the three]

The author is using the image of the **head** to represent a leader or commander. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the commander of]

nt: The author is using the adjectives **three** and **second** as nouns. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjective with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [From the three warriors in the second rank, he was honored]

The author is using the term **From** to introduce a comparison. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. You could also use plain language. Alternate translation: [Of the three warriors in the second rank, he was the most honored]

The expression **was honored** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that would be natural in your language. Alternate translation: [People honored him the most of the three warriors in the second rank] or [People honored him the most of the next three of David’s greatest warriors]

If your language would not represent a number in a form such as **second**, you could represent this number in a form that your language would use, or you could use an equivalent expression. Alternate translation: [in rank two] or [next greatest warriors]

Here, **come to** represents joining or achieving the same level of status as the Three. The verse means that although Abishai was a great warrior and was highly honored, he did not achieve membership in or equal status with the Three. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly, here and in verse 25. Alternate translation: [But he did not join the ranks of the Three] or [But he did achieve the same exploits and reputation as the Three]

he author is using **a man of measure** as a common expression of his culture to mean a giant. The author is using the phrase **five by the cubit** to express height in a way characteristic of his culture. Alternate translation: [five cubits tall]

A **cubit** was an ancient unit of measurement corresponding to the distance between an average person’s elbow and middle fingertip, or about 46 centimeters or 18 inches. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could express this man’s height in modern measurements, either in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [seven and a half feet tall]
